z-m-17-01.title: If sectors have arcs of the same length, do they also have the same area?
z-m-17-01.topic: Arc length and area of a sector
z-m-17-01.goal: Judge whether the condition that the arc lengths are equal alone decides a sector's area, check by making examples with different radii, and explain how arc length and area each change with the radius and the central angle.
z-m-17-01.material:
At a school festival booth, sector-shaped paper decorations are made. A gold ribbon with a length of 6π cm is attached to the curved part (the arc) of each decoration. The radius and central angle can be chosen differently for each decoration. (π is pi, and the thickness of the paper and ribbon is ignored. The central angle is greater than 0° and less than 360°.)
Mina said, "If the ribbon length is the same, 6π cm, the areas of the paper decorations must all be the same."
z-m-17-01.thinking.0: Sorting out when a generalization holds and when it does not
z-m-17-01.thinking.1: Making several examples yourself that satisfy the conditions
z-m-17-01.thinking.2: Explaining why two quantities change differently with the same variable
z-m-17-01.prereq.0: Circumference and area of a circle, and that a sector's arc length and area are directly proportional to its central angle (grade 7 level)
z-m-17-01.prereq.1: That π (pi) is the ratio of a circle's circumference to its diameter
z-m-17-01.s.s1.prompt: Before calculating, choose what you think now about Mina's statement.
z-m-17-01.s.s1.hint.0: Picture two decorations with the same ribbon length. Imagine the case where their radii are the same and the case where they are different.
z-m-17-01.s.s1.hint.1: Think about what must happen to the central angle to make an arc of the same length when the radius is made larger.
z-m-17-01.s.s1.o.a: Always right. If the ribbon length is the same, the decorations have the same shape
z-m-17-01.s.s1.r.a: You thought that once the ribbon length is set, the radius and central angle are set as one pair. Since arc length is decided by the radius and central angle together, check whether there are cases where the two values differ but the arc length is the same.
z-m-17-01.s.s1.o.b: Always wrong. Two decorations with the same ribbon length always have different areas
z-m-17-01.s.s1.r.b: This judgment misses two decorations with the same radius. Check what happens to the two decorations when the radius is also the same.
z-m-17-01.s.s1.o.c: Can't tell now. We can judge only if the central angle is given
z-m-17-01.s.s1.r.c: You thought it is hard to judge unless values are given. But a question like 'is it always the same?' can be tested by making examples, without fixing a single value.
z-m-17-01.s.s1.o.d: It depends on the case. Sometimes it is the same and sometimes it is different
z-m-17-01.s.s1.r.d: You thought that you must sort out in which cases it is the same and in which it is different. Check those cases with examples.
z-m-17-01.s.s1.explain: At first, 'it depends on the case' is the most suitable judgment. If the radius is the same, the central angle is also the same and the decorations are identical, but if the radius is different, they can differ. Now let's make examples and check.
z-m-17-01.s.s2.prompt: Make 3 sector decorations with ribbon length 6π cm that have different radii. (radius r cm, central angle x°)
z-m-17-01.s.s2.hint.0: First decide what relation between r and x makes the expression for the arc length equal 6π.
z-m-17-01.s.s2.hint.1: Pick an r, fit x, and then calculate the arc length directly to check that it is 6π.
z-m-17-01.s.s2.ok.c1: The radius is positive and the central angle is greater than 0° and less than 360°.
z-m-17-01.s.s2.fail.c1: The radius must be greater than 0 and the central angle must be greater than 0° and less than 360° for it to be a sector.
z-m-17-01.s.s2.fail.c2: The arc length is not 6π cm. Put r and x into the expression for arc length and check directly whether it is 6π.
z-m-17-01.s.s2.explain: With radius 6 cm and central angle 180°, the area is 18π cm²; with radius 12 cm and central angle 90°, it is 36π cm²; with radius 18 cm and central angle 60°, it is 54π cm². Even with the same ribbon length, if the radius is different, the area is different.
z-m-17-01.s.s3.prompt: Answer Mina. Choose two of the decorations you made above, compare their areas, and write why the areas differ even though the ribbon length is the same.
z-m-17-01.s.s3.hint.0: Among the decorations you made, choose the two whose radii differ the most and write each one's area.
z-m-17-01.s.s3.hint.1: For the two decorations, compare side by side how many times greater the radius became and how many times greater the area became.
z-m-17-01.s.s3.placeholder: e.g., The decoration with radius ... has ...
z-m-17-01.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you compare the radius, central angle, and area of both decorations using numbers?
z-m-17-01.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Along with saying 'the area differs,' did you write the reason (that the radius differs)?
z-m-17-01.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you also think about what happens when the ribbon length is the same and the radius is the same?
z-m-17-01.s.s3.model.0: Even with the same ribbon length, the area differs. The decoration with radius 6 cm and central angle 180° has area 18π, but the decoration with radius 12 cm and central angle 90° has 36π, double. When the radius gets larger, even if the central angle gets smaller, the area gets larger.
z-m-17-01.s.s3.model.1: 'Always the same' is wrong. Even using the same 6π cm ribbon, with radius 9 the central angle is 120° and the area is 27π, and with radius 18 the central angle is 60° and the area is 54π, so they differ. Only decorations with the same radius have the same area.
z-m-17-01.s.s3.modelNote.1: It is an answer that connects to the first judgment, 'it depends on the case.'
z-m-17-01.s.s3.model.2: Area of sector = ½ × r × arc length = 3πr, so even if the arc lengths are the same, the larger the radius, the larger the area.

z-m-17-02.title: Finding the wrong line in a solution for the angle between clock hands
z-m-17-02.topic: Size of angles and units: the angle made by clock hands
z-m-17-02.goal: Find and fix the wrong line in a solution for the angle made by clock hands, and explain that when both hands move, each hand's position must be set separately to match the time.
z-m-17-02.material:
On the face of an analog clock, 12 numbers are placed at equal intervals, and angles are measured clockwise from the 12 o'clock direction. The clock is accurate and each hand turns at a constant rate. The hour hand makes one turn in 12 hours, and the minute hand makes one turn in 60 minutes. Minjae tried to find the angle made by the hour hand and minute hand at 3:20 (the smaller of the two angles) and solved it as below.
1) One full turn of the clock is 360° and there are 12 numbers, so one number space is 30°.
2) The minute hand makes one turn in 60 minutes, so it goes 6° per minute, and at 20 minutes it is 120° from the 12 o'clock direction.
3) The hour hand is pointing at 3, so it is 90° from the 12 o'clock direction.
4) The angle between the two hands is 120° − 90° = 30°.
5) Therefore the angle made by the hour hand and minute hand at 3:20 is 30°.
z-m-17-02.thinking.0: Checking each line of a solution against the situation
z-m-17-02.thinking.1: Finding the wrong line and finding the result again with the corrected value
z-m-17-02.thinking.2: Explaining the cause of an error to another person
z-m-17-02.prereq.0: Expressing the size of an angle in degrees (°) and that a full turn is 360°
z-m-17-02.prereq.1: How to read an analog clock
z-m-17-02.s.s1.prompt: Choose one wrong line in Minjae's solution.
z-m-17-02.s.s1.hint.0: Match the hand positions written in each line, one by one, with the real look of the clock at 3:20.
z-m-17-02.s.s1.line.0: One full turn of the clock is 360° and there are 12 numbers, so one number space is 30°.
z-m-17-02.s.s1.line.1: The minute hand makes one turn in 60 minutes, so it goes 6° per minute, and at 20 minutes it is 120° from the 12 o'clock direction.
z-m-17-02.s.s1.line.2: The hour hand is pointing at 3, so it is 90° from the 12 o'clock direction.
z-m-17-02.s.s1.line.3: The angle between the two hands is 120° − 90° = 30°.
z-m-17-02.s.s1.line.4: Therefore the angle made by the hour hand and minute hand at 3:20 is 30°.
z-m-17-02.s.s1.explain: Line 3 is wrong. At 3:20 the hour hand does not stay at the 3 o'clock position; while the minute hand goes around for 20 minutes, it has moved a little further too. The hour hand makes one turn (360°) in 12 hours, so it goes 30° per hour, and in 20 minutes it goes 10° more, so it is 100° from the 12 o'clock direction. Lines 4 and 5 use line 3's value as it is, so their calculations are right but the result changes.
z-m-17-02.s.s2.prompt: If you fix Minjae's solution correctly, how many degrees is the smaller angle made by the hour hand and minute hand at 3:20?
z-m-17-02.s.s2.hint.0: First work out the angle the hour hand moves in one hour (60 minutes).
z-m-17-02.s.s2.hint.1: Use that value to find the angle the hour hand moved in 20 minutes, rewrite the hour hand's position, and compare it with the minute hand's position.
z-m-17-02.s.s2.r.b: You compared the positions of the two hands again, including how far the hour hand moved in 20 minutes.
z-m-17-02.s.s2.r.c: You brought over the first solution as it is, which saw the hour hand as staying at the 3 o'clock position.
z-m-17-02.s.s2.r.d: You read the hour hand's position (the angle from the 12 o'clock direction) as the angle between the two hands. You need the value compared with the minute hand's position.
z-m-17-02.s.s2.explain: The hour hand is at 100° and the minute hand is at 120°, so the angle between the two hands is 20°. As another method, you can use the fact that the minute hand goes 5.5° per minute faster than the hour hand and get the same value (at 3 o'clock the minute hand is 90° behind the hour hand, and in 20 minutes it catches up 110°, so it is ahead by 20°).
z-m-17-02.s.s3.prompt: Write a note to send to Minjae. Explain how line 3 should be fixed, together with the reason it must be fixed that way.
z-m-17-02.s.s3.hint.0: Compare whether the hour hand is in the same position at 3 o'clock sharp and at 3:20.
z-m-17-02.s.s3.hint.1: Use how many degrees the hour hand goes in an hour to find the angle it went in 20 minutes.
z-m-17-02.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you write in numbers how much farther the hour hand went from 3?
z-m-17-02.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you go on to write how the angle between the two hands changes when that value is put in?
z-m-17-02.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you consider what thinking might have made Minjae write line 3 that way?
z-m-17-02.s.s3.model.0: The hour hand also moves a little while the minute hand turns, so at 3:20 it is at the 100° position, 10° beyond 3. So if you fix line 3 to 100°, it is 120°−100°=20°.
z-m-17-02.s.s3.model.1: The hour hand goes 30° per hour, so in 20 minutes it goes 10° more. Line 3 should be fixed to 90°+10°=100°, and then the angle between the two hands is 20°, not 30°.
z-m-17-02.s.s3.modelNote.1: It is an answer that wrote out the calculation steps.
z-m-17-02.s.s1.hint.1: Draw a clock at exactly 3 o'clock and a clock at 3:20, and compare which of the two pictures the hand positions described in each line match.
z-m-17-02.s.s2.r.a: You read as the answer only the angle (10°) that the hour hand moved in the extra 20 minutes. The angle between the two hands is a value found by comparing the positions of the hour hand and the minute hand.
z-m-17-02.s.s3.model.2: The hour hand moves 0.5 degrees per minute, so in 20 minutes it moves 10 degrees more. So line 3 should be corrected to 100 degrees.
z-m-17-02.s.s3.modelNote.2: An answer explained with the angle moved per minute.

z-m-17-03.title: To fill a sphere-shaped bowl, how many times do we need the water from a cone bowl?
z-m-17-03.topic: Volume of a sphere: the relation among the volumes of a sphere, a cone, and a cylinder
z-m-17-03.goal: Estimate the relation among the volumes of a sphere, a cone, and a cylinder before calculating, revise the estimate each time a measurement result comes in and sort it out into an exact ratio, and gauge how many times greater the volume becomes when lengths are doubled.
z-m-17-03.material: There is a sphere-shaped bowl A with radius 3 cm, a cone-shaped bowl B with base radius 3 cm and height 6 cm, and a cylinder-shaped bowl C with base radius 3 cm and height 6 cm. Sphere A fits inside cylinder C touching the top, bottom, and side exactly. Let's say the thickness of the bowls is ignored and no water is spilled. The sizes of the bowls are told again at each step of this task.
z-m-17-03.thinking.0: Separating what is certain from what is a guess with what you know now
z-m-17-03.thinking.1: Revising judgment and certainty with new data
z-m-17-03.thinking.2: Being careful when generalizing from one measurement
z-m-17-03.prereq.0: The volume of a cylinder (base area × height), and that the volume of a cone with the same base and height is one third of the cylinder's
z-m-17-03.prereq.1: You do not need to know the formula for the volume of a sphere (it is found in this task)
z-m-17-03.s.s1.prompt: Data is revealed one piece at a time. At each step, choose what you think is most suitable with only what is known now, and when new data comes in, continue or revise your judgment.
z-m-17-03.s.s1.hint.0: At each step, separate what you can say for certain from only what is known so far from what is just a guess.
z-m-17-03.s.s1.hint.1: Taking cylinder C as the reference, draw or imagine the parts that sphere A and cone B take up, and compare them.
z-m-17-03.s.s1.st.0.info: There are three bowls. A is sphere-shaped with radius 3 cm, B is cone-shaped with base radius 3 cm and height 6 cm, and C is cylinder-shaped with base radius 3 cm and height 6 cm. Sphere A fits inside cylinder C touching the top, bottom, and side exactly. The thickness of the bowls is ignored and no water is spilled. The volume of a cone with the same base and height is one third of the cylinder's volume.
z-m-17-03.s.s1.st.0.ask: You try to fill A completely by filling B with water and pouring it into A, repeating this. Before calculating, how many pourings do you think are needed for A to be full?
z-m-17-03.s.s1.st.0.after: Sphere A fits inside cylinder C and there is empty space near the corners, so you can say it takes fewer than 3 times of B, the amount that fills C. You can't yet know exactly how many times.
z-m-17-03.s.s1.st.0.o.a: It seems A will be full after pouring about 3 times, with nothing short
z-m-17-03.s.s1.st.0.r.a: You thought the sphere fills the cylinder completely. Picture the empty parts between the sphere and the corners of the cylinder.
z-m-17-03.s.s1.st.0.o.b: It seems pouring more than 1 time and fewer than 3 times will do
z-m-17-03.s.s1.st.0.r.b: You guessed it is more than one bowl of the cone but not as much as the cylinder. Say what the comparison is that backs this up.
z-m-17-03.s.s1.st.0.o.c: It seems even pouring 1 time is enough to fill it
z-m-17-03.s.s1.st.0.r.c: You treated the sphere and the cone as the same size. Compare the part each takes up inside the cylinder.
z-m-17-03.s.s1.st.0.o.d: It won't exceed 3 times, but we need to calculate to know the exact number of times
z-m-17-03.s.s1.st.0.r.d: You thought that the range is known but the exact number of times needs calculation or measurement.
z-m-17-03.s.s1.st.1.info: We actually measured. When we filled B with water and poured it into A twice, A was filled exactly. (No water was spilled and the bowls are considered to have no thickness.)
z-m-17-03.s.s1.st.1.ask: What is the most suitable way to accept this measurement result?
z-m-17-03.s.s1.st.1.after: From the measurement, A is 2 times B and cylinder C is 3 times B. So A is two thirds of C. You can also check by calculation. B is 18π, A is 36π, and C is 54π cm³. However, to say that one measurement applies to all sizes, you need to check at other sizes too.
z-m-17-03.s.s1.st.1.o.a: A is 2 times B and C is 3 times B, so A is two thirds of C
z-m-17-03.s.s1.st.1.r.a: You connected the measurement result with the relation between cylinder and cone and read out even the relation between sphere and cylinder.
z-m-17-03.s.s1.st.1.o.b: A is half of C, because the sphere fits the cylinder exactly
z-m-17-03.s.s1.st.1.r.b: You felt that since the sphere fits the cylinder exactly, it would be half. Compare with the fact that in the measurement A is 2 times B and C is 3 times B.
z-m-17-03.s.s1.st.1.o.c: We can only know that A is 2 times B and cannot know the relation with C
z-m-17-03.s.s1.st.1.r.c: You did not use the relation between cylinder and cone that was given along with the measurement. Connect the two facts.
z-m-17-03.s.s1.st.1.o.d: We measured only one case, so we have to check separately whether it is the same at other sizes
z-m-17-03.s.s1.st.1.r.d: This is a careful attitude toward generalizing from one measurement. Along with this judgment, you can also state the relation you have found now.
z-m-17-03.s.s1.st.2.info: Now we make bowls with all lengths doubled. A' is a sphere with radius 6 cm, and C' is a cylinder with base radius 6 cm and height 12 cm. A' also fits exactly inside C'.
z-m-17-03.s.s1.st.2.ask: How many times A's volume is the volume of A′?
z-m-17-03.s.s1.st.2.after: The volume of cylinder C' is π×6²×12 = 432π, which is 8 times C's 54π. A' is two thirds of C', so 288π, and A is 36π, so it is 8 times. When lengths are doubled, width, depth, and height all double, so the volume becomes 2×2×2 = 8 times.
z-m-17-03.s.s1.st.2.r.a: You thought that when lengths double, the volume doubles too. Compare the volumes of cylinders C' and C directly.
z-m-17-03.s.s1.st.2.r.b: This is the value of multiplying 2 twice, like an area. For volume, all three directions, width, depth, and height, are involved.
z-m-17-03.s.s1.st.2.r.c: This took into account that all three directions double.
z-m-17-03.s.s1.st.2.r.d: This is the value of multiplying 2 four times. Check how many directions you need to multiply.
z-m-17-03.s.s1.reflect: At first you could only say the range 'fewer than 3 times,' from the measurement you learned the relation 2 : 3, and at the end you gauged how many times the volume becomes when lengths are enlarged. Look back at what certainty grew or shrank at each step and what evidence caused it.
z-m-17-03.s.s2.prompt: Sua said, "A sphere fits exactly in a cylinder, so the sphere's volume must be half the cylinder's." Evaluate whether this is right using the measurement results above as evidence, and if it is not right, write how it should be fixed.
z-m-17-03.s.s2.hint.0: From the measurement results, write one line each for the relation of A, B, and C in terms of 'how many times.'
z-m-17-03.s.s2.hint.1: Calculate how many bowls of B the 'half' Sua mentioned corresponds to and compare it with the measurement result.
z-m-17-03.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you base your answer on the measurement results (A is 2 times B, C is 3 times B)?
z-m-17-03.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you separate the part of Sua's guess that is right (the sphere is smaller than the cylinder) from the part that is wrong (half)?
z-m-17-03.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Did you write the corrected statement (for example, a fraction) clearly in numbers?
z-m-17-03.s.s2.model.0: That's not right. Pouring B twice fills A, and C takes 3 times of B, so A is two thirds of C. It is right that the sphere is smaller than the cylinder, but it is much more than half.
z-m-17-03.s.s2.model.1: A is 36π and C is 54π cm³, so A÷C = 2/3. Even though the sphere fits the cylinder exactly, the corners are empty, so it is not full, but it fills two thirds, not half. Sua's guess needs to be fixed.
z-m-17-03.s.s2.modelNote.1: It is an answer that compared volumes in numbers.

z-m-17-04.title: What do we need to know to find the angle between the bisectors of two angles?
z-m-17-04.goal: Tell apart the information needed from the information lacking to decide the angle made by two bisectors, make several cases that give the same value, and explain the condition under which the statement 'always 90°' holds.
z-m-17-04.material: Rays OA, OB, and OC extend from point O. OB lies between OA and OC, so ∠AOC = ∠AOB + ∠BOC, and ∠AOC is greater than 0° and at most 180°. Ray OM bisects ∠AOB (divides it into two angles of the same size), and ray ON bisects ∠BOC. What we want to know is the size of ∠MON.
z-m-17-04.thinking.0: Judging whether the information is enough
z-m-17-04.thinking.1: Making several cases that satisfy the conditions
z-m-17-04.thinking.2: Giving a counterexample and stating the condition for a generalization
z-m-17-04.prereq.0: The meaning of an angle bisector
z-m-17-04.s.s1.prompt: We want to decide the size of ∠MON. Among the following, choose all those for which knowing only that information lets you decide ∠MON.
z-m-17-04.s.s1.hint.0: For each piece of information, look for and test whether there is a picture that keeps the information but gives ∠MON different values.
z-m-17-04.s.s1.hint.1: Write in words which smaller angles ∠MON is made of.
z-m-17-04.s.s1.r.a: Knowing only one angle, you don't know how much ∠BOC is. Compare ∠MON in the case where ∠AOB is 40° and ∠BOC is 20° and in the case where it is 100°.
z-m-17-04.s.s1.r.b: Look at whether, if you know both angles, you can decide all four small angles made by the two bisectors.
z-m-17-04.s.s1.o.c: Only that ∠BOC is 2 times ∠AOB is known
z-m-17-04.s.s1.r.c: This is the case where only the ratio of the two angles is known and not the sizes. Compare ∠MON when ∠AOB is 20° and when it is 40°.
z-m-17-04.s.s1.o.d: Only that OB bisects ∠AOC is known
z-m-17-04.s.s1.r.d: You only know the two angles are equal. Check whether this information does not decide whether each is 40° or 70°.
z-m-17-04.s.s1.o.e: That ∠AOC = 140° and the rest is unknown
z-m-17-04.s.s1.r.e: Look for the reason you do not need to know ∠AOB and ∠BOC separately in what angles ∠MON is made of.
z-m-17-04.s.s1.explain: OM and ON bisect ∠AOB and ∠BOC respectively, so ∠MON = ½∠AOB + ½∠BOC = ½∠AOC. So you can decide it by knowing the two angles each, or by knowing only the sum ∠AOC. If you know only one angle, only the ratio of the two angles, or only that the two angles are equal, you cannot decide it.
z-m-17-04.s.s2.prompt: Decide, in 3 different ways, the sizes (a, b) of ∠AOB and ∠BOC so that ∠MON is exactly 70°. (Ones where ∠AOB and ∠BOC are swapped count as the same.)
z-m-17-04.s.s2.hint.0: First decide one ∠AOB and fit ∠BOC so that ∠MON is 70°.
z-m-17-04.s.s2.hint.1: Add the small angles divided by the angle bisectors directly and check that they make 70°.
z-m-17-04.s.s2.ok.c1: Both angles are positive and ∠AOC is at most 180°.
z-m-17-04.s.s2.fail.c1: Both angles must be greater than 0°, and the sum (∠AOC) must be at most 180°.
z-m-17-04.s.s2.fail.c2: ∠MON is not 70°. Add directly the small angles that the two bisectors each make and check.
z-m-17-04.s.s2.explain: If a+b = 140, then ∠MON = 70°. For example, with 40° and 100°, 20°+50°=70°, and with 70° and 70°, 35°+35°=70°.
z-m-17-04.s.s3.prompt: Jeonghun said, "∠MON made by the two bisectors is always 90°." Give one example where this is not right, and write when ∠MON is 90°, together with the reason.
z-m-17-04.s.s3.hint.0: Choose one of the (a, b) you made above, write ∠MON, and check whether it equals 90°.
z-m-17-04.s.s3.hint.1: Compare the sizes of ∠MON and ∠AOC for a few pairs and look for the rule between them.
z-m-17-04.s.s3.placeholder: e.g., If ∠AOB is ... and ∠BOC is ..., then ...
z-m-17-04.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you give an example with ∠AOB, ∠BOC, and ∠MON all written in numbers?
z-m-17-04.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you connect what size ∠AOC must be for ∠MON to be 90° with the fact that it is half?
z-m-17-04.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you rewrite Jeonghun's statement as being right only in certain cases, not 'always'?
z-m-17-04.s.s3.model.0: Jeonghun's statement is not always right. If ∠AOC is 140°, ∠MON is half of it, 70°. For it to be 90°, ∠AOC must be 180° (A, O, C on one straight line). ∠MON is always half of ∠AOC.
z-m-17-04.s.s3.model.1: No. If ∠AOB=40° and ∠BOC=100°, then ∠MON=20°+50°=70°. Only when ∠AOB and ∠BOC add up to 180° is half of it 90°. It happens only for a straight angle that forms a straight line.
z-m-17-04.s.s3.modelNote.1: It gave an example that added the small angles directly.

z-m-17-05.title: Is the middle of two classes' means the overall mean?
z-m-17-05.topic: Mean: the mean of two groups combined
z-m-17-05.goal: Judge whether the overall mean can be decided from the two classes' means alone, find combinations of numbers of students that give the same overall mean, and explain with numbers why the mean tilts toward the side with more students.
z-m-17-05.material: Class A and class B took the same math test. Class A's mean is 70 points and class B's mean is 80 points. We want to know the overall mean of both classes' students combined. Both classes have at least 1 student, and say a class has at most 40 students. Doyun said, "(70+80)÷2 = 75, so the overall mean is 75 points."
z-m-17-05.thinking.0: Judging when a calculation method holds
z-m-17-05.thinking.1: Making several cases that satisfy the conditions
z-m-17-05.prereq.0: Mean = sum of the values ÷ number of values
z-m-17-05.prereq.1: Setting up an expression using the letters a, b (grade 7 level)
z-m-17-05.s.s1.prompt: Choose what you think is most suitable about Doyun's calculation. (We don't yet know the numbers of students in the two classes.)
z-m-17-05.s.s1.hint.0: Set the numbers of students in the two classes (a case where they are equal, and a case where one is much larger) and work out the total of all the scores.
z-m-17-05.s.s1.hint.1: Recall that the mean is 'sum of scores ÷ number of students,' and first write each class's sum of scores.
z-m-17-05.s.s1.o.a: Only when the two classes have the same number of students is the overall mean 75 points
z-m-17-05.s.s1.r.a: You worked out when the simple average of the two classes' means equals the overall mean.
z-m-17-05.s.s1.o.b: Regardless of the numbers of students in the two classes, the overall mean is always 75 points
z-m-17-05.s.s1.r.b: You thought the mean of the means is the overall mean. Think about whether the scores of the class with more students count more in the whole.
z-m-17-05.s.s1.o.c: Class B's scores are higher, so the overall mean is always higher than 75 points
z-m-17-05.s.s1.r.c: You looked only at class B having the higher mean. Test the case where class A has many more students.
z-m-17-05.s.s1.o.d: Only that it is higher than 70 and lower than 80 is certain, and the exact value depends on the numbers of students
z-m-17-05.s.s1.r.d: You stated for certain the range that it lies between the two means. Also work out when, within that range, it would be 75 points.
z-m-17-05.s.s1.explain: If class A has a students and class B has b students, the overall mean is (70a+80b)÷(a+b). For this value to be 75, a=b is needed. If the numbers of students differ, it tilts toward the class with more students.
z-m-17-05.s.s1.acc.0: This is also true. The overall mean lies between the two means and depends on the numbers of students. It would be even better to go further and state the condition for 75 points (when the numbers of students are equal).
z-m-17-05.s.s2.prompt: Find 3 different pairs of numbers of students (class A a students, class B b students) for which the overall mean is exactly 78 points. (A class has from 5 to 40 students.)
z-m-17-05.s.s2.hint.0: When class A has a students and class B has b students, write the total of all scores and the total number of students using a and b.
z-m-17-05.s.s2.hint.1: Set up an equation from the sum and the number of students for the overall mean being 78 points, and find the relation between a and b.
z-m-17-05.s.s2.ok.c1: Both classes have a natural number of students from 5 to 40.
z-m-17-05.s.s2.fail.c1: Please make the number of students a natural number from 5 to 40.
z-m-17-05.s.s2.fail.c2: The overall mean is not 78 points. Calculate directly the sum of the two classes' scores divided by the total number of students.
z-m-17-05.s.s2.explain: With 5 students in class A and 20 in class B, (70×5+80×20)÷25 = 1950÷25 = 78 points. When class B has 4 times as many students as class A, the overall mean is 78 points.
z-m-17-05.s.s3.prompt: Explain to Doyun. Write why the overall mean is not 75 points when the two classes have different numbers of students, showing one of the examples you found above with numbers.
z-m-17-05.s.s3.hint.0: Choose one of the (a, b) you found above and write each class's sum of scores.
z-m-17-05.s.s3.hint.1: Compare whether the overall mean is closer to 70 or to 80, and how many students that class has.
z-m-17-05.s.s3.placeholder: e.g., If class A has ... students and class B has ... students, ...
z-m-17-05.s.s3.selfAssess.0: In your example, did you write both classes' numbers of students and the overall mean in numbers?
z-m-17-05.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you say that the overall mean gets close to the mean of the class with more students?
z-m-17-05.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you also point out that it is 75 points when the numbers of students are equal?
z-m-17-05.s.s3.model.0: If class A has 20 students and class B has 40, the sum of scores is 70×20+80×40=4600 and there are 60 students, so the mean is about 76.7 points. It is closer to class B, which has more students, so it is not 75 points.
z-m-17-05.s.s3.model.1: Adding the two means and halving is right only when the numbers of students are equal. For example, with 10 students in class A and 40 in class B, there are more students in class B, so it gets pulled toward 80 points, and the overall mean is 78 points.
z-m-17-05.s.s3.modelNote.1: It is an answer that connects to the example above (78 points).

z-m-17-06.title: If the sum of relative frequencies came out to 0.99, is the table wrong?
z-m-17-06.topic: Relative frequency: rounding and the sum
z-m-17-06.goal: Learn how to check whether a gap in the sum of relative frequencies from 1 is due to rounding or a real error, revise judgment and certainty with new information, and make a table yourself in which the sum is off because of rounding.
z-m-17-06.material: In a frequency distribution table, the sum of the relative frequencies is 1. However, in a table where the relative frequencies are written rounded, the sum can be slightly off from 1. In this task, relative frequencies are written rounded to two decimal places.
z-m-17-06.thinking.0: Sorting out and checking the cause of a gap
z-m-17-06.thinking.1: Revising judgment and certainty to fit new information
z-m-17-06.thinking.2: Making several tables that satisfy the conditions
z-m-17-06.prereq.1: Relative frequency = frequency of a class ÷ total frequency
z-m-17-06.prereq.2: How to round to two decimal places
z-m-17-06.s.s1.prompt: Data is revealed one piece at a time. At each step, choose what you think is most suitable with only what is known now, and when new data comes in, continue or revise your judgment.
z-m-17-06.s.s1.hint.0: At each step, write separately what you have already checked and what you have not checked yet.
z-m-17-06.s.s1.hint.1: Work out about how many times the difference made by rounding one value the size of the gap in the sum is.
z-m-17-06.s.s1.st.0.info:
For 30 students, a frequency distribution table was made by dividing the number of books read in one week into three classes, and each class's relative frequency (that class's frequency ÷ total frequency) was written rounded to two decimal places.
Class / Frequency / Relative frequency
0 books or more, less than 2 books / 10 students / 0.33
2 books or more, less than 4 books / 10 students / 0.33
4 books or more, less than 6 books / 10 students / 0.33
Total / 30 students / 0.99
z-m-17-06.s.s1.st.0.ask: The relative frequency in the total cell is 0.99, not 1. How will you treat this table now?
z-m-17-06.s.s1.st.0.after: From the fact that the sum is not 1 alone, you cannot say it is wrong or that it is fine. You need to check for what reason it is off.
z-m-17-06.s.s1.st.0.o.a: There might be a calculation mistake, so recalculate the frequencies and relative frequencies and check
z-m-17-06.s.s1.st.0.r.a: This is the attitude of rechecking the part you doubt. What you will judge after checking is what matters.
z-m-17-06.s.s1.st.0.o.b: The difference might come from rounding, so examine the values directly
z-m-17-06.s.s1.st.0.r.b: This is the attitude of keeping open that there may not be only one cause and checking.
z-m-17-06.s.s1.st.0.o.c: The sum of relative frequencies must be 1, so this table, which is not 1, is a wrong table
z-m-17-06.s.s1.st.0.r.c: The property that the sum is 1 is about the values before rounding. Work out whether it applies as is to values shortened to two decimal places.
z-m-17-06.s.s1.st.0.o.d: A 0.01 difference is very small, so rewrite the total as 1.00 without checking
z-m-17-06.s.s1.st.0.r.d: If you fix it without knowing why even a small difference arose, you cannot tell a real error from a rounding difference.
z-m-17-06.s.s1.st.1.info: When checked, the frequencies were 10, 10, 10, and their sum equaled the total of 30 students. Each relative frequency is 10÷30 = 0.3333..., and it was written rounded to two decimal places as 0.33. Everything below the third decimal place was dropped.
z-m-17-06.s.s1.st.1.ask: Seeing this result of the check, what is the most suitable judgment about this table?
z-m-17-06.s.s1.st.1.after: If you shorten 0.3333... at the third decimal place, all three values become slightly smaller, so the sum is 0.99. This kind of difference is due to rounding, not to the table being wrong. There is also a way to adjust a value to make the sum 1, but in that case you must state that you adjusted it.
z-m-17-06.s.s1.st.1.o.a: The calculation is right. The sum became 0.99 because of the difference from dropping everything below the third decimal place
z-m-17-06.s.s1.st.1.r.a: You judged by connecting the result of checking the calculation with the effect of rounding.
z-m-17-06.s.s1.st.1.o.b: Even if the calculation is right, if the sum is not 1 it is a wrong table, so the frequencies must be set again
z-m-17-06.s.s1.st.1.r.b: You saw it as wrong even though the calculation is right. Think about what you get when you shorten 0.3333... and add it three times.
z-m-17-06.s.s1.st.1.o.c: The calculation is right. You may write one value as 0.34 to make the sum 1, but state that you adjusted it
z-m-17-06.s.s1.st.1.r.c: You thought about the fact that there is a way to make the sum fit and also that you must state it then.
z-m-17-06.s.s1.st.1.o.d: Change the frequencies to something like 10, 10, 11 so the sum gets close to 1
z-m-17-06.s.s1.st.1.r.d: A frequency is the result of counting students. You must not change the data to make the table's sum fit.
z-m-17-06.s.s1.st.2.info: There is another group's table. All 30 students were divided into four classes, and the frequencies are written as 4, 6, 8, 15. Each relative frequency was written rounded to two decimal places as 0.13, 0.20, 0.27, 0.50, and 1.10 was written in the total cell.
z-m-17-06.s.s1.st.2.ask: What is the most suitable judgment about the total of 1.10 in this table?
z-m-17-06.s.s1.st.2.after: The sum of the frequencies is 4+6+8+15 = 33, which differs from the total of 30 students. Rounding one value changes it by at most about 0.005, so the sum of four values can be off by at most about 0.02. 1.10 is far larger than that, so it is not rounding; the frequencies or the total number of students is wrong.
z-m-17-06.s.s1.st.2.o.a: It is a difference caused by rounding, just like the earlier table, so this table is also considered a right table
z-m-17-06.s.s1.st.2.r.a: You saw it as the same reason as the earlier table. Compare whether this difference is the same size as the earlier difference.
z-m-17-06.s.s1.st.2.o.b: There are as many as four classes, so rounding differences alone can make the sum 1.10
z-m-17-06.s.s1.st.2.r.b: It is right that rounding errors can pile up in the sum. But compare with how small the difference from a single value is.
z-m-17-06.s.s1.st.2.o.c: A rounding difference can hardly give 0.10, so check whether the sum of the frequencies is 30
z-m-17-06.s.s1.st.2.r.c: You compared the size of the difference with rounding error and decided where to check.
z-m-17-06.s.s1.st.2.o.d: Even if the sum is not 1, it is fine as long as each relative frequency is right, so don't worry about the total cell
z-m-17-06.s.s1.st.2.r.d: This judgment misses what information the value in the total cell gives. Think about what could be going on when the sum is far off.
z-m-17-06.s.s1.reflect: The same phenomenon, the sum not being 1, is sometimes due to rounding and sometimes a real error. Look back at whether you told them apart by checking if the size of the difference is of a degree rounding can explain and whether the sum of the frequencies matches the total.
z-m-17-06.s.s2.prompt: Choose frequencies (a, b, c) of three classes with total frequency 30, and make 3 different tables in which, when each relative frequency is rounded to two decimal places and added, the sum is not 1.00. (Ones where only the order of the classes is changed count as the same table.)
z-m-17-06.s.s2.hint.0: Pick a frequency, find the relative frequency to three decimal places, and then round it to two decimal places.
z-m-17-06.s.s2.hint.1: Add all three rounded relative frequencies and check whether the sum equals 1.00.
z-m-17-06.s.s2.ok.c1: The three frequencies are natural numbers and their sum is 30 students.
z-m-17-06.s.s2.fail.c1: The three frequencies must be natural numbers that are at least 1 and their sum must be 30.
z-m-17-06.s.s2.ok.c2: The sum of the rounded relative frequencies (seen as percentages) is not 1.00 (100%).
z-m-17-06.s.s2.fail.c2: With these frequencies, the sum of the rounded relative frequencies is 1.00. Find each relative frequency to two decimal places and add them directly.
z-m-17-06.s.s3.prompt: A friend in your group says, "If the sum of relative frequencies is not 1, it's a wrong table no matter what." Write how you would correct this statement, together with a way to tell wrong tables from ones that are not.
z-m-17-06.s.s3.hint.0: Put the two tables from the earlier steps side by side and compare the size of the gap of the sum from 1.
z-m-17-06.s.s3.hint.1: Write separately what to check when the gap is small and when it is large.
z-m-17-06.s.s3.placeholder: e.g., It isn't that if the sum is not 1, then ...
z-m-17-06.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you give examples of the difference caused by rounding (0.99, 1.01, etc.)?
z-m-17-06.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you write what to check when the sum is far off?
z-m-17-06.s.s3.selfAssess.2: In what words did you correct 'wrong no matter what'?
z-m-17-06.s.s3.model.0: It isn't wrong no matter what just because the sum is not 1. If you round to two decimal places, 0.33 added three times can be a little short, like 0.99. Add the frequencies again and check that they match the total; if the difference is about 0.01 to 0.02 it is because of rounding, and if it is large like 0.1 it is wrong.
z-m-17-06.s.s3.model.1: Because of rounding, the sum can be 0.99 or 1.01. First recalculate each relative frequency yourself and see whether the sum of the frequencies equals the total frequency. If both are right and it is slightly off, the table is right.
z-m-17-06.s.s3.modelNote.1: It is an answer that wrote the order of checking.

z-m-17-07.title: If scores are adjusted by the same rule, how do the mean and the gaps between scores change?
z-m-17-07.topic: Mean, median, range: when scores are changed by a fixed rule
z-m-17-07.goal: Learn how the representative values and the spread each change when all values are changed by adding the same number or multiplying by the same number, and make adjustment rules yourself that satisfy conditions and compare them.
z-m-17-07.material: The math unit test was hard, so the mean came out low. The teacher wants to adjust all students' scores by the same rule. The original scores of 7 students are 35, 50, 55, 55, 65, 70, 90 points, and the mean is 60 points, the median is 55 points, the mode is 55 points, and the difference between the highest and lowest scores is 55 points. The adjusted score is found as 'original score × p + q' (p is a number greater than 0), and a score cannot exceed 100 points.
z-m-17-07.thinking.0: Reasoning about the rule of change
z-m-17-07.thinking.1: Designing a rule that satisfies several conditions at once
z-m-17-07.prereq.0: Finding the mean, median, mode, and the difference between the largest and smallest values of data
z-m-17-07.prereq.1: Putting numbers into an expression with letters (p × score + q) to find its value
z-m-17-07.s.s1.prompt: Rule A: Add 8 points to every student's score. Choose everything that stays the same as the original after adjusting.
z-m-17-07.s.s1.hint.0: Write the 7 new scores yourself by adding 8 to the 7 original scores.
z-m-17-07.s.s1.hint.1: Compare the mean, median, mode, and the difference between the highest and lowest scores of the original scores and the new scores.
z-m-17-07.s.s1.o.a: The mean value of the 7 students' scores
z-m-17-07.s.s1.r.a: Check whether you accounted in the mean for the fact that if all scores go up by 8 points, the sum of the scores increases.
z-m-17-07.s.s1.o.b: The middle value when the 7 students' scores are put in order of size (the median)
z-m-17-07.s.s1.r.b: Think about whether the middle score in size order is also the score raised by the same 8 points.
z-m-17-07.s.s1.o.c: The difference between the highest and lowest scores
z-m-17-07.s.s1.r.c: Look at what happens to the difference between two scores when they both go up by the same amount.
z-m-17-07.s.s1.o.d: The value that appears most often among the 7 students' scores (the mode)
z-m-17-07.s.s1.r.d: Think about whether the score that appears most often is also the score raised by 8 that appears most often.
z-m-17-07.s.s1.o.e: Who is how-manyth highest, the order of the scores
z-m-17-07.s.s1.r.e: Check whether adding the same score to everyone changes who is higher.
z-m-17-07.s.s1.explain: If you add 8 points to every score, the mean 60 points → 68 points, the median 55 points → 63 points, and the mode 55 points → 63 points, all going up by 8 points. The gaps between scores stay the same, so the difference between the highest and lowest scores (55 points) and the order of the scores do not change.
z-m-17-07.s.s2.prompt: Set the adjustment rule as 'original score × p + q.' Find 3 different rules (p, q) that satisfy all of the following. ① The mean after adjusting is exactly 75 points. ② The highest score after adjusting is 100 points or less. ③ The difference between the highest and lowest scores after adjusting is at least half of the original (55 points).
z-m-17-07.s.s2.hint.0: The mean is the value of applying the same rule to the original mean of 60 points. Decide what relation between p and q is needed for this value to be 75.
z-m-17-07.s.s2.hint.1: Pick a p, fit q, and apply the rule to the highest score 90 points and the lowest score 35 points to check the two conditions.
z-m-17-07.s.s2.ok.c1: p is greater than 0, so the order of scores is kept.
z-m-17-07.s.s2.fail.c1: p must be greater than 0 for the order of scores to be kept.
z-m-17-07.s.s2.ok.c2: The mean after adjusting is 75 points.
z-m-17-07.s.s2.fail.c2: The mean after adjusting is not 75 points. Check whether applying the same rule to the original mean of 60 points gives 75.
z-m-17-07.s.s2.ok.c3: The highest score is 100 points or less.
z-m-17-07.s.s2.fail.c3: Applying the rule to the original highest score of 90 points goes over 100 points.
z-m-17-07.s.s2.ok.c4: The difference between the highest and lowest scores is at least 27.5 points.
z-m-17-07.s.s2.fail.c4: The difference between the highest and lowest scores after adjusting is less than 27.5 points. Apply the rule to the original two scores (90 points, 35 points) and find the difference.
z-m-17-07.s.s2.explain: With p=0.8, q=27, the scores become 55, 67, 71, 71, 79, 83, 99 points, so the mean is 75 points, the highest score is 99 points, and the difference is 44 points. With p=0.6, q=39, the mean is 75 points, the highest score is 93 points, and the difference is 33 points. The smaller p is than 1, the narrower the gaps between scores get, and q raises everything.
z-m-17-07.s.s3.prompt: Choose one of the rules you found and compare it with rule A (adding 8 points). Explain with numbers what the difference between the scores of a high-scoring student and a low-scoring student becomes under each rule.
z-m-17-07.s.s3.hint.0: With the rule you chose, rewrite the highest score 90 points and the lowest score 35 points after changing them.
z-m-17-07.s.s3.hint.1: Compare the difference between the two changed scores with 55 points and work out how many times it became.
z-m-17-07.s.s3.placeholder: e.g., I chose the rule with p=..., q=.... The highest score 90 points ...
z-m-17-07.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you find the highest and lowest scores under your chosen rule in numbers?
z-m-17-07.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you compare that under rule A the difference stays the same and under your rule it changes?
z-m-17-07.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you explain how much the difference changed in connection with p?
z-m-17-07.s.s3.model.0: I chose the rule of multiplying by 0.8 and adding 27 points. The highest score 90 points becomes 99 points and the lowest score 35 points becomes 55 points, so the difference between them shrinks from 55 points to 44 points. If you only add 8 points, the difference stays 55 points, but with the multiplying rule, the gaps between scores get narrower.
z-m-17-07.s.s3.model.1: With p=0.6, q=39, the highest score is 93 points and the lowest score is 60 points, so the difference shrinks to 33 points. Adding 8 points keeps the difference at 55 points, so the gaps do not change, but with my rule, the gaps between all scores become 0.6 times.
z-m-17-07.s.s3.modelNote.1: It is an answer that said the difference becomes p times.
